---
title: "Shrinking correlated coefficients"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

**Ridge regression** adds a squared-coefficient penalty to the least-squares objective:

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^{\,\text{ridge}}(\lambda)
=
\arg\min_{\beta_0,\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\sum_i
\left(y_i-\beta_0-\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta\right)^2
+\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2
\right].
$$

The intercept is left unpenalized. When predictors are on different scales, standardization must be estimated from the training data so that the penalty is comparable across columns.

## New-item validation in MALD

We use log frequency, log duration, phone count, and syllable count to predict a new MALD item summary. Every item occurs once in the table, so assigning folds by item is also a row split. `glmnet` estimates standardization separately inside each training-fold fit.

```{r}
#| label: validate-mald-ridge
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnet)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-items.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
X <- model.matrix(
  ~ log_frequency_subtlex + log_duration + n_phones + n_syllables,
  data = mald
)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
y <- mald$mean_log_rt

n_folds <- 10L
set.seed(20261020)
fold_id <- sample(rep(seq_len(n_folds), length.out = nrow(mald)))
penalty_grid <- 10^seq(-5, 1, length.out = 80L)
ridge_mixing <- 0
fold_mse <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_folds, ncol = length(penalty_grid))
ridge_predictions <- matrix(
  NA_real_,
  nrow = nrow(mald),
  ncol = length(penalty_grid)
)
ols_predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(mald))

for (fold in seq_len(n_folds)) {
  training <- fold_id != fold
  testing <- !training

  ridge_fit <- glmnet(
    x = X[training, , drop = FALSE],
    y = y[training],
    alpha = ridge_mixing,
    lambda = penalty_grid,
    standardize = TRUE,
    intercept = TRUE
  )
  current_predictions <- predict(
    ridge_fit,
    newx = X[testing, , drop = FALSE],
    s = penalty_grid
  )
  ridge_predictions[testing, ] <- current_predictions
  fold_mse[fold, ] <- colMeans((y[testing] - current_predictions)^2)

  ols_fit <- lm(
    mean_log_rt ~ log_frequency_subtlex + log_duration +
      n_phones + n_syllables,
    data = mald[training, ]
  )
  ols_predictions[testing] <- predict(ols_fit, newdata = mald[testing, ])
}

mean_mse <- colMeans(fold_mse)
se_mse <- apply(fold_mse, 2, sd) / sqrt(n_folds)
minimum_index <- which.min(mean_mse)
one_se_candidates <- which(
  mean_mse <= mean_mse[minimum_index] + se_mse[minimum_index]
)
one_se_index <- max(one_se_candidates)
lambda_min <- penalty_grid[minimum_index]
lambda_one_se <- penalty_grid[one_se_index]
ridge_one_se_prediction <- ridge_predictions[, one_se_index]

ridge_rmse <- sqrt(mean((y - ridge_one_se_prediction)^2))
ols_rmse <- sqrt(mean((y - ols_predictions)^2))

stopifnot(
  nrow(mald) == length(unique(mald$item)),
  all(is.finite(ridge_one_se_prediction)),
  all(is.finite(ols_predictions)),
  lambda_one_se >= lambda_min
)

data.frame(
  method = c("ridge: one-SE rule", "ordinary least squares"),
  held_out_rmse = c(ridge_rmse, ols_rmse)
)
```

The minimum-error penalty is `r format(lambda_min, digits = 4)`, while the one-standard-error penalty is `r format(lambda_one_se, digits = 4)`. The new-item RMSE is `r sprintf("%.6f", ridge_rmse)` for the one-SE ridge fit and `r sprintf("%.6f", ols_rmse)` for OLS.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-ridge-validation
#| fig-cap: "New-item validation error across the ridge penalty grid. The solid and dashed lines mark the minimum-error and one-standard-error choices."
validation_curve <- data.frame(
  lambda = penalty_grid,
  rmse = sqrt(mean_mse)
)

ggplot(validation_curve, aes(lambda, rmse)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lambda_min, color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = lambda_one_se,
    color = "black",
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Ridge penalty", y = "New-item cross-validated RMSE") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Ridge does not beat OLS in this comparison. That outcome is part of the lesson: shrinkage changes the bias--variance tradeoff, but it does not guarantee lower predictive loss in a particular dataset.

## Check your understanding

1. Which coefficients are penalized?
2. Why must standardization be learned inside each training fold?
3. What is the held-out unit?
4. What does the observed OLS--ridge comparison show?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. All non-intercept predictor coefficients are penalized; the intercept is left unpenalized. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Full-data standardization uses held-out predictor values to set the penalty scale, so validation no longer evaluates a purely training-fitted new-item procedure and its error estimate may be biased. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. One MALD word item is held out; because every item appears once, the item split is also a row split. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. In these fixed folds, one-SE ridge has higher new-item RMSE than OLS, so shrinkage does not improve this observed prediction comparison. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
